summary: Provides a model and requirements for message tracking, the ability to learn the path a message has taken through a messaging system and its current status. It was written to answer a common customer question about enterprise messaging systems.

plainLanguage.summary: Message tracking means finding out which mail servers a message has passed through and what its current status is. RFC 3888 describes the parts of a mail system that would be involved, the rules any tracking service has to follow, and the different ways a tracking service can be switched on and queried.

questions: how can i track an email message
who is allowed to track an email
subtitle: A model and a list of requirements for finding out where an email has been and what happened to it.

tldr.problem: Customers buying enterprise messaging systems ask the same question: can I track my messages? There was no common description of what a message tracking service does, so the answer differed from one vendor to the next.
tldr.mechanism: The memo names every part of a mail system, sets out what a tracking solution must be able to do, and gives two ways to turn tracking on and two ways to ask for the result, with the information each can return.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that specifies no protocol. It states that a tracking solution must be reachable only by the person who sent the message, and it sketches an authentication scheme for proving that.

facts.label: Random number in the second scheme

today: RFC 3888 is an Informational memo published in September 2004, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a model and a set of requirements rather than a protocol, and points at three companion documents for the security details: RFC 3885, RFC 3886 and RFC 3887.

sections.title: Why Message Tracking
sections.content:
The memo starts from a question that customers buying enterprise message systems ask: can I track the messages? Message tracking is the ability to find out the path that a particular message has taken through a messaging system and the current routing status of that message.

The comparison the memo draws is with sending a package through a package delivery company. Once you have sent a package, you would like to know whether it has been delivered, and if not, where it currently is and what its status is. The status of a package may not include whether it was delivered to its addressee, but only the destination. Many package carriers provide such services today, often through a web interface. Message tracking extends that capability to the Internet-wide message infrastructure: the ability to quickly locate where a message is, and to determine whether it has been delivered to its final destination.

The memo argues that an Internet-standard approach will allow the development of message tracking applications that operate in a multi-vendor messaging environment, and will encourage the operation of the function across administrative boundaries. It provides a model of message tracking that can be used for understanding the Internet-wide message infrastructure, and requirements for proposed message tracking solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo answers a question that enterprise buyers keep asking: can I find out where my message is right now? It says a tracking service should be able to say which mail servers a message has passed through, whether it has reached its destination, and what its state is at each step.

sections.title: The Parts of a Mail System
sections.content:
The memo gathers the vocabulary it needs, and marks two of the terms as new. The originating Mail User Agent (MUA) is the software used to compose and originate a message, the software sitting on a person's desktop. The Mail Submission Agent (MSA) accepts a message from a user agent, adds or modifies it as required for Internet standards and/or site policy, and injects the message into the network. The MSA may be the initial MTA or may hand the message off to an MTA. A Message Transfer Agent (MTA) accepts a message and moves it forward towards its destination, which may be local or reached via another MTA. It may use a local queue to store the message before transferring it further, and any MTA may generate a Non-Delivery Notification.

An Intermediate MTA is an MTA that accepts a message for transfer somewhere else. A Final MTA is an MTA that accepts a message for local delivery; it is the final place a message is accepted, and it is what sends any Delivery Status Notifications. A Foreign MTA provides delivery of messages using other protocols than those specified for Internet mail, such as an X.400 mail system, and a Gateway MTA accepts a message for transfer to a foreign MTA outside the Internet protocol space. A Local Delivery Agent delivers the message to the local message store, and the MTA and LDA are often combined into the same program.

A Delivery Status Notification (DSN) is produced by an MTA when a message is unsuccessfully delivered, either to its next hop or the final message store, or when it is successfully delivered to a foreign MTA, a local delivery agent or a non-DSN aware MTA. Positive notifications are only performed when specifically requested. A Non-Delivery Notification (NDN) is a special form of DSN indicating unsuccessful delivery, and a Message Disposition Notification (MDN) reports the disposition of a message after it has been successfully delivered to a recipient.

The two new terms are the Tracking User Agent (TUA), which wants to find information on a message on behalf of a user and is the requestor or initiator of such a request, and the Tracking Server, which provides tracking information to a tracking client and is the repository of the information about a message for the traversal through a particular MTA. The MUA and the TUA could be combined into the same program, and the tracking server and the MTA may run on the same system. Section 3 lists the entities involved in message tracking: message user agents, message submission agents, message transfer agents, tracking user agents and tracking servers.
sections.plainLanguage: A message usually passes through several programs before it arrives. The memo names each one: the program you write in, the program that hands it to the network, the servers that relay it, and the server that puts it in the recipient's mailbox. Two new names are added: the tracking user agent that asks the questions, and the tracking server that holds the answers.

sections.title: Requirements for a Tracking Solution
sections.content:
The memo lists the requirements that any message tracking solution must be able to satisfy.

It MUST scale to the Internet, and it MUST be easy to deploy. It SHOULD maximize the reuse of existing, already deployed technology and infrastructure, and, if possible, SHOULD extend existing protocols and not invent new ones. It SHOULD have a low implementation cost, which makes it easy to incorporate into existing products.

On access, the solution MUST restrict tracking of a message to the originator of the message, or to a delegate. It MAY allow an originator to delegate this responsibility to a third party, and SHOULD have the property that it would allow per-message delegation of the tracking responsibility. A tracking user agent MUST be required to prove that it is permitted to request the tracking information.

On identification, the solution MUST be able to uniquely identify messages, and it MUST require every message to have unique identification.
sections.plainLanguage: Two of these rules are about privacy: only the person who sent a message, or someone they name, may ask about it, and asking has to be proved. The rest are practical: the system must work at Internet scale, must be cheap to add to products that already exist, and must not invent a new protocol if an existing one will do.

sections.title: Turning Tracking On and Asking for the Result
sections.content:
Tracking has to be enabled before it can be asked for. Either the envelope or the message header must contain enough information to track a message and securely retrieve information about it. Any message that does not have enough information to track it is by definition not trackable. If there is not enough information in the current standard envelopes or message headers, then the current standards will need to be extended: either the MUA or the MSA must determine the additional information and enable tracking by adding it to either the envelope or the header. That leads to two enabling models. In the passive enabling model there is assumed to be sufficient information available, no user agent or submission agent interaction occurs to turn tracking on, and it is on by default. In the active enabling model the MUA and MSA exchange information when the message is submitted, indicating that logging of the message's traversal should be performed and providing enough additional information to allow the message to be tracked; that information is then passed on to subsequent MTAs as needed.

There are also two models for asking. The passive request model requires active enabling to indicate that some form of tracking is to be performed, and the tracking information can be sent back immediately, as a form of telemetry, or sent to a third party for later retrieval. The information that can be asked for includes a DSN of a message arriving at an intermediate MTA, a DSN of a message being rejected while at an intermediate MTA, a DSN of a message leaving an intermediate MTA and going to another MTA, a DSN of a message arriving at a final MTA, a DSN of a message being rejected while at a final MTA, a DSN of a message being delivered to a user's message store, a DSN of a message being delivered to a foreign MTA, and an MDN of a message being read by an end user. Mechanisms already exist for most of these, through RFC 3464, RFC 2852 and RFC 3798.

The active request model requires an active query by a user's user agent to the MSA, the intermediate MTAs and the final MTA, or to a third party, to find the message's status as known by that MTA. It works with either passive enabling or active enabling. The information that can be asked for this way includes whether the message has been queued for later delivery, whether it was delivered locally, whether it was delivered to another MTA, whether it was delivered to a foreign MTA, and whether to ask a different tracking server. Two further answers are possible: the server knows but cannot say, and the server does not know. No mechanisms currently exist for requesting this information.

When a tracking server is asked for information and the message has been passed on to another MTA that it has no tracking knowledge for, there are two modelling choices. The first tracking server can contact the next tracking server to query for status and pass back the combined status, which is called server chaining, or it can return the address of the next MTA and leave the tracking client to contact the next tracking server, which is called server referral.

Finally, the memo notes that the information retrieved by message tracking and the information returned for DSN and MDN requests all attempt to answer the same question, what happened to message XX. The information provided by each is complementary in nature but similar, and a tracking user agent could use all three possible information sources to present a total view of the status of a message. Both DSN and MDN notifications use the formats defined by RFC 3462, which suggests that the information returned by message tracking solutions should be similar.
sections.plainLanguage: Tracking can be switched on in two ways. It can simply be on, with the message carrying enough information from the start, or the sending program and the first server can agree to turn it on and pass the extra information along. Asking works in two ways too: the server can send the status out as it happens, or a program can ask each server in turn what it knows.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo summarises the security vulnerabilities of message tracking, which are detailed in RFC 3885, RFC 3886 and RFC 3887. They include vulnerability to snooping or replay attacks when using unencrypted sessions, a dependency on the randomness of the per-message secret, reliance on TLS, man-in-the-middle attacks, reliance on the server maintaining the security level when it performs chaining, denial of service, confidentiality concerns, and forgery by malicious servers.

It then offers a possible security model for message identification and authentication. A Tracking User Agent must prove that it is permitted to request tracking information about a message, and every RFC 822 compliant message is supposed to contain a Message-Id header. One possible mechanism is for the originator to calculate a one-way hash A from the message ID, a time stamp and a per-user secret, and then to calculate another one-way hash B that is the hash of A. The user includes B in the submitted message and retains A. Later, when the user makes a message tracking request, the user submits A, and the entity receiving the request uses A to calculate B, since it was already provided B, which verifies that the requestor is authentic. In short, A = H(message ID + time stamp + secret) and B = H(A).

Another possible mechanism for A is to ignore the message ID and time stamp and use a one-way hash from a large random number of more than 128 bits, with B calculated as before. This is similar in technique to the one-time password methods of RFC 2289. The success of these techniques depends on the randomness of the per-user secret or the large random number, which can be incredibly difficult in some environments. If the originator of a message delegates the tracking request to a third party by sending it A, that would be vulnerable to snooping over unencrypted sessions, and the user can decide on a message-by-message basis whether that risk is acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: The risks are the ones you would expect from a system that reports on a message in flight: someone could listen in, someone could pretend to be a tracking server, and the whole thing could be flooded with requests. The memo's answer to impersonation is that the sender keeps a secret, puts a hash of it in the message, and shows the original when asking for the status.

messages.label: TRACKING REQUEST
messages.note: The tracking user agent asks for the status of a message, and proves that it is allowed to ask.

messages.label: STATUS QUERY
messages.note: In the server chaining model the first tracking server queries the next one itself.

messages.label: STATUS
messages.note: The next server answers with what it knows about the message, which may be that it does not know.

messages.label: COMBINED STATUS
messages.note: The first server passes the combined status back. In the referral model it returns the address of the next MTA instead and the client contacts it.
